lead: Every closed boundary has corners. Once each corner has an easting and a northing, the area inside comes from one sum of cross products. You walk around the boundary in order, multiply each easting by the change in northing, and add. The method is used for land records, plot layout, earthwork and GIS. It needs no drawing and no scale. The only rules are: keep the corners in order, finish the loop, and remember that the raw sum is twice the area.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.4 for coordinates and Chapter 2.5 for adjusted coordinates; Unit 1 covers area units.

blocks.text: Let every corner have coordinates (E, N): E is easting, the distance east of the origin, and N is northing, the distance north. Both in metres. Number the corners 1 to n in order around the boundary. For corner i, write E<sub>i</sub> and N<sub>i</sub>. The next corner is i+1; the previous is i−1. At the ends wrap around: corner n+1 is corner 1, and corner 0 is corner n.

blocks.where: A is the area in square metres; E<sub>i</sub> is the easting of corner i; N<sub>i+1</sub> and N<sub>i−1</sub> are the northings of the next and previous corners; the sum runs once around all n corners.

blocks.text: The same area has a second form. It pairs each corner with the next one directly:

blocks.where: E<sub>i</sub>, N<sub>i</sub> are the coordinates of corner i; E<sub>i+1</sub>, N<sub>i+1</sub> are those of the next corner; the last pair uses corner 1 after corner n.

blocks.text: Both formulas return twice the area, not the area. A table keeps the work visible. For the first form, write one row per corner with columns E, N, next N, previous N, and the product E × (next N − previous N). Add the product column. Divide the total by 2. The result is the area, provided the coordinates and the order are correct.

items: List the corners in boundary order.
For each row, read the next and previous northings.
Multiply the easting by their difference.
Add all rows and halve the total.

blocks.text: Take the corners in one direction around the boundary, clockwise or anticlockwise. Do not jump across the plot, skip a corner or repeat the first corner at the end. A jump makes the figure cross itself like a bow-tie. The formula then adds some outside parts and subtracts inside parts, so the number is not the plot area.

The sign of the sum fixes the direction. With eastings to the right and northings up, an anticlockwise walk gives a positive sum; a clockwise walk gives a negative sum. Area is never negative: take the absolute value. The sign is information about the direction, not a reason to drop the result.

Keep both coordinates in the same unit before multiplying. If E and N are in metres, the sum is in square metres and A = S/2 is in square metres, where S is the raw sum and A is the area. Convert at the end. 1 hectare = 10 000 m². 1 acre = 4046.86 m². For example, 550 m² is 550 ÷ 10 000 = 0.055 ha.

Double meridian distance (DMD) is the older name for the same job done from latitudes and departures. The double area is the sum of DMD × latitude for every line, with signs; halve it for the area. The coordinate formula is the shorter modern route.

The coordinates may come from a closed traverse after adjustment, from a total station, or from a GNSS receiver. In all three cases the arithmetic is the same. The coordinates must refer to one consistent grid and one consistent unit. An adjusted traverse is preferred because the closing error has already been spread; see Chapter 2.5. Coordinate computation is the step that produces these E and N values; the area step starts only after they are fixed.

CAD and GIS compute the same sum in an instant. A polygon area command uses this cross-product rule, not a planimeter or a grid count. For a surveyor, the formula is still needed to check the software, to show the method in an exam, and to understand why the order of points matters. It is used in land records, plot layout, land acquisition, and any map overlay that reports an area; see Unit 7 for GIS analysis. One wrong point moves one product and changes the area, so check the order and the unit before trusting the total.

figure.caption: The corners are in boundary order. The last column is E × (N_next − N_prev); its total 1100 is twice the area, so the plot is 550 m².

spec.title: Corners in order, eastings and northings in m; last column = E × (N_next − N_prev)
spec.aria: A coordinate table for the four corners of a plot with the cross-product term for each corner and a total of 1100, which is twice the area.

examples.question: Find the area of the plot ABCD with corners A(10, 10), B(30, 10), C(40, 30) and D(20, 40), eastings and northings in metres, taken in order around the boundary. Check the answer with the other form of the formula.
steps: Write the coordinates in order. A: E = 10 m, N = 10 m. B: E = 30 m, N = 10 m. C: E = 40 m, N = 30 m. D: E = 20 m, N = 40 m. There are n = 4 corners.
At A, next is B with N = 10 m, previous is D with N = 40 m. Product = 10 × (10 − 40) = −300 m².
At B, next is C with N = 30 m, previous is A with N = 10 m. Product = 30 × (30 − 10) = 600 m².
At C, next is D with N = 40 m, previous is B with N = 10 m. Product = 40 × (40 − 10) = 1200 m².
At D, next is A with N = 10 m, previous is C with N = 30 m. Product = 20 × (10 − 30) = −400 m².
Sum S = −300 + 600 + 1200 − 400 = 1100 m². This S is twice the area, so area A = 1100 ÷ 2 = 550 m².
examples.answer: The area of plot ABCD is 550 m², which is 0.055 ha.
examples.check:
pts = [(10, 10), (30, 10), (40, 30), (20, 40)]
n = len(pts)
s = 0
for i, (E, N) in enumerate(pts):
    Nn = pts[(i + 1) % n][1]
    Np = pts[(i - 1) % n][1]
    s += E * (Nn - Np)
cross = 0
for i in range(n):
    E1, N1 = pts[i]
    E2, N2 = pts[(i + 1) % n]
    cross += E1 * N2 - E2 * N1
assert s == cross
area = abs(s) / 2
ha = area / 10000
print(area)
print(ha)

traps: Taking corners out of order, or skipping one, makes a bow-tie; the sum is not the area.
Reporting the raw sum as the area. The formulas give twice the area; divide by 2.
Forgetting the wrap-around: the first corner uses the last northing as previous, and the last uses the first northing as next.
Mixing easting and northing, or mixing metres with millimetres, in the same table.
Turning a negative sum into negative area. Take the magnitude; the sign only shows clockwise travel.

quiz.q: Write the coordinate formula for twice the area using E and (N_next − N_prev).
quiz.a: 2A = Σ E_i (N_{i+1} − N_{i−1}) taken once around the boundary, with wrap-around at the ends.

quiz.q: Why must the corners be listed in boundary order?
quiz.a: The formula assumes each row follows the previous one. Jumping or skipping gives a self-crossing bow-tie and a wrong area.

quiz.q: A triangle has A(0, 0), B(40, 0) and C(0, 30) m. Find its area by coordinates.
A student obtains raw sum −900 m². What is the area and the travel direction?
quiz.a: Area = 900 ÷ 2 = 450 m². Negative sign means clockwise travel under the east-right, north-up convention.

quiz.q: Convert 0.055 ha to m² and to acre.
Why is the raw sum called twice the area?
quiz.a: The cross-product identity gives twice the polygon area. Halving the sum is part of the formula, not an extra correction.

quiz.q: The same four corners are walked clockwise and anticlockwise. Compare the raw sums and the areas.
quiz.a: The raw sums are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign. Both give the same positive area after taking the absolute value and halving.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern GIS stores each parcel as a polygon and recomputes the shoelace sum after every edit, so cadastral records can be kept area-consistent. Drone photogrammetry produces thousands of boundary points; the same formula turns them into a stockpile or field area. A useful next search is the shoelace formula, and then polygon area computation in QGIS or PostGIS. Surveyors also meet it inside coordinate geometry tools and land record software.
